response: Waiting without knowing why someone is late can feel lonely, and it makes sense that you felt unimportant. It's also worth knowing that a train cancellation stopped B from taking the planned train, so the delay had an outside cause. It doesn't seem to show how B feels about the dinner. When B arrived and seemed annoyed, that may have come from a stressful trip, but only B can say. You could share how the wait felt for you, then ask B what the journey was like. You might also agree on a quick way to let each other know about delays next time.

It sounds stressful to stand on that platform, anxious and wanting to get to dinner, and then to arrive to silence. The train cancellation really did stop you from taking your planned train, and you tried to send word. I can't say why A went quiet, since I only have your side. A might not have gotten your message, or might have felt something you don't know about yet. When things are calmer, you could tell A what happened on your end, then ask what the wait was like for them and really listen to the answer.

It sounds like you each had a hard evening, and you were each missing part of the picture. A, you waited without knowing about the train cancellation, so feeling unimportant makes sense. B, you were anxious on the platform, wanted to get there, and tried to send a message that may not have reached A. When you met, A saw annoyance and B felt shut out. Neither of you was there for the other's experience. It may help to tell each other what those 30 minutes were like for you, and then agree on a backup plan for times when messages might not get through.

It sounds like you each had a hard evening, in different ways. B, a cancelled train kept you from the train you'd planned on, and you felt anxious and wanted to get there. A, you didn't know about the cancellation, so the wait felt like a sign you didn't matter. That was a painful reading, and an understandable one given what you knew. When you met, each of you saw the other as cold or annoyed. It may help to talk through what each of you felt that night. You could also agree on a backup way to reach each other, like a call, for when plans go wrong.

Feeling rejected when someone you care about heads straight to another room makes sense, especially if it has happened before and left you on edge. Your feeling is real. What isn't settled yet is why B did it. Anger is one possibility, but people also step away to decompress after a long day, to finish a call, or just to get some quiet. Since the two of you never agreed on how to greet each other, try asking calmly. You could say something like, "When you go straight to the other room, I feel shut out. What's going on for you then?" Asking that way opens the door to understanding without assuming the worst.

It sounds like the noise at work left you overloaded, and the twenty minutes alone gave you a quiet interval so you could be present for A afterward. That's a caring reason, even if it may not have looked that way from the outside. We only have your side here, so we don't know how A felt about it. Since you two never set an explicit agreement about greetings, it could help to name the habit together. A quick 'I'm home, I need a few quiet minutes, then I'm all yours' can keep your recovery time from being misread.

A, feeling rejected when B walked away is understandable, especially since you had no agreement about how to greet each other. B describes that time differently. B says it wasn't anger. B felt overloaded by noise at work and wanted a short quiet break so they could be present for you afterward. Neither account has to be wrong. One way forward is a simple shared plan, such as a quick hello and a word like 'I need ten minutes' before stepping away. A could also check in when it feels like anger rather than assuming. That way, B's need for quiet doesn't land as rejection.

It sounds like those twenty minutes landed very differently for each of you. B, you describe needing quiet after a noisy day so you could be present afterward. A, you felt rejected and read it as anger. B's account doesn't mention anger, so that may be worth checking directly instead of assuming. Since you have no agreement about greetings, a small one could help both of you. For example, B could give a quick hello and say 'I need a few minutes to decompress' before stepping away. A could then share what kind of reconnection feels good afterward.

Feeling taken for granted makes sense when an agreement isn't kept. You'd planned on B handling the dishes, and seeing them in the sink the next morning stung. Still, the facts only show that the dishes stayed out overnight. They don't show why. B might have forgotten, been worn out, run out of time, or something else. Since you haven't asked yet, try opening with curiosity instead of a conclusion. You could say, "We'd agreed you'd do the dishes last night, and seeing them this morning left me feeling taken for granted. What happened?" Then you can deal with what actually happened.

It makes sense that a long, important call pushed the dishes out of your mind. That happens. It's also clear you'd agreed to do them that evening, and they sat in the sink overnight. Both of those are true. You may feel annoyed that A doesn't see why you were distracted, but A may simply have noticed the agreement wasn't kept. It could help to say, 'I forgot, and I'm sorry. The call took over.' Then wash them, or agree on a time to do it. Owning the slip usually makes it easier for A to understand the reason behind it.

It sounds like you both ended up frustrated over something small that touched bigger feelings. A, seeing the dishes made you feel taken for granted, but you didn't check what happened. B, you say you forgot after an important call, which is understandable, though you had agreed to do them. A quick, calm conversation could help. B might acknowledge the missed commitment and explain the call. A might share how it felt without assuming intent. You could also agree on what to do next time plans slip, like sending a short message or handling it first thing in the morning.

It sounds like a small thing that turned into a bigger hurt on both sides. B, you say you forgot after an important call, and that matters. Still, the dishes were your agreed task, and A ended up facing them in the morning. A short acknowledgment might go further than asking A to understand. A, feeling taken for granted makes sense, but you haven't yet heard what happened. Asking B directly could change how it looks to you. You might both agree on a simple backup plan for when something urgent comes up, such as a quick text saying you'll do them in the morning.

It makes sense that you felt disappointed. You had pictured Saturday as your time together, and it turned out differently. Still, the two of you hadn't actually agreed to spend that afternoon together, and you each made your own plans. Nothing here shows why B made theirs, so the idea that B was avoiding you is a guess, not something you know. It may help to tell B that you'd been hoping for that time together and ask how they saw the day. Making shared time something you plan together could head off this kind of mismatch next time.

It makes sense that the disagreement surprised you. You both made separate plans, and you hadn't agreed to spend Saturday afternoon together, so your understanding had a real basis. We don't have A's side, though, so it's unclear what A expected or why it bothered them. Calling A 'always so sensitive' might make it harder for A to explain. You could try asking something like, 'What were you hoping Saturday would look like?' Then the two of you could agree on how you'll check plans with each other next time.

It sounds like you each brought a different expectation to Saturday without saying so. A, you assumed the afternoon was shared and felt disappointed. B, you thought you were both making separate plans and were surprised by the disagreement. Nothing here shows that B planned things to avoid A, or that A is 'always' sensitive. Those are interpretations that may make the conversation harder. A useful next step might be to talk openly about how you each want to handle weekends and to agree on shared time ahead of time, so neither of you has to guess.

It sounds like you each brought a different expectation to Saturday. A, you assumed it was time together. B, you understood your plans as separate. Neither of you had actually agreed on it. A, your disappointment makes sense. Still, nothing here shows that B was trying to avoid you, and asking B about it may help more than guessing at motives. B, your surprise is understandable too. Calling A 'always so sensitive' may make things harder, though. Naming the specific moment usually works better. Going forward, it could help to talk openly about how you'd like to spend weekends, so neither of you is left relying on assumptions.

Feeling worried during four hours of silence makes sense, especially when you can't tell whether your message was even read. Still, nothing here shows why B didn't reply, or whether B saw the message at all. B could have been busy, away from the phone, or something else entirely. Before you settle on an explanation, try a calm check-in. You might say, 'I noticed I hadn't heard back and got a little worried. Is everything okay?' That way you share how you felt without guessing at B's reasons. It also gives B a chance to explain.

B, it sounds like you were caught between two real needs: concentrating on your work and not wanting A to feel ignored. Keeping your phone in your bag while you work is a reasonable choice. A four-hour gap can still feel long to the person waiting, though. One option is to agree with A ahead of time. You could tell A when you'll be heads-down, or send a quick "busy, will reply later" note. Both of those let you focus and still show A that you care. It might also help to ask A how the silence felt from their side.

A, it makes sense that four hours of silence felt worrying, especially since you couldn't tell whether B had read the message. B, you were focused on work with your phone in your bag, and you didn't want A to feel ignored. Neither account suggests bad intentions. It sounds more like the two of you have different expectations about how quickly to reply. You might agree on a simple habit. For example, B could send a quick note like "heads down working, talk later," and A could check in again if something is urgent. That way, focus and reassurance can both fit into the day.

It sounds like you both had understandable experiences. A, four hours of silence with no sign the message had been read naturally left room for worry. B, keeping your phone in your bag to focus on work makes sense, and you say you didn't want A to feel ignored. Nothing here shows bad intent on either side. It might help to agree on a small signal for busy stretches. That could be a quick 'heads-down, will reply later' note or a shared idea of how long a gap usually means nothing is wrong. Then focus time doesn't turn into uncertainty.

Feeling upset when your partner questioned something you meant as helpful for you both makes sense. You've also been honest that you knew the 120-unit purchase fell under your agreement to discuss anything over 100 first, and that's a good place to start. When you talk with B, you could acknowledge that you skipped the agreed step, then explain why you thought the item would help you both. You might also ask how it felt for B to find out afterward. Keeping the hurt and the agreement as two separate topics can make it easier to rebuild trust and stop the conversation from turning into blame.

B, it makes sense that you felt excluded. You both agreed to talk before spending over 100 units, and this 120-unit purchase happened without that conversation. That concern is real and worth raising. Words like "always" and "impulsive" may make it harder for A to hear you, though. It could help to focus on this specific purchase and what you need going forward. For example, you could agree on how to check in quickly when timing feels tight. A's view isn't included here, so asking what led to the decision could open a more productive conversation.

You both agree on the basic facts. The purchase was 120 units, over your agreed threshold, and it wasn't discussed first. A, you say you knew about the agreement, and you also felt upset when it was questioned. B, you felt left out of the decision. That makes sense, since the agreement exists to prevent exactly that. B, your view that A is 'always' impulsive goes further than this one incident shows. Sticking to this purchase may help the conversation. It could also help to talk about whether the agreement still works for both of you, and what A could do next time when something seems useful but goes over the limit.

A, the purchase was 120 units, and you agreed to discuss anything over 100 first. You've said yourself that you knew this. B, you felt left out of a decision about money you share. That is a reasonable thing to feel. Words like 'always' and 'impulsive' sum up a whole person, though, and that can make A defensive instead of willing to listen. What happened this time was one missed check-in, and you can fix that. A could own the slip without arguing about whether the item is useful. B could say how this affected you and ask for what you need. Then you could both agree on how to handle the next purchase over 100.

It makes sense that you felt let down. You reached out and heard nothing back, and that silence can easily feel like being avoided. What actually happened, though, is that a fan blew the note behind a cabinet before B came into the room. B never saw it that evening, so the lack of a reply wasn't B dodging you. It might help to tell B what the note said, and to mention that the silence hurt. Then B can respond to the real message and the situation can be sorted out directly.

Your confusion makes sense. The note blew behind a cabinet before you came in, so you had no way to see it or respond to it. That doesn't mean A's frustration came from nowhere. From A's side, it may have felt like a message was ignored. It could help to calmly share what actually happened, maybe even look behind the cabinet together. Then ask A what the note said and what they were hoping for. That way you can both talk about the real need rather than the misunderstanding.

It sounds like a fan caused this, not either of you. The note blew behind the cabinet before B came in, so B never saw it. A, it makes sense you felt let down when you heard nothing back, but the silence wasn't B avoiding you. B, your confusion makes sense too, since you were hearing about a note you didn't know existed. Maybe check behind the cabinet together and read the note then. Next time, a quick text that says 'left you a note' could keep a stray breeze from turning into a misunderstanding.

It sounds like this was a painful mix-up, not an act of avoidance. A fan blew the note behind a cabinet before B came in, so B never saw it. A, your disappointment makes sense: you reached out and heard nothing back, and that hurts. B, your confusion makes sense too, since you were reacting to something you didn't know existed. You might start by finding the note together, or by A sharing what it said. Then talk about what A was hoping to hear. For important messages, it could help to check in directly as well as leaving a note.

Thank you for sharing this. You said clearly that you wanted to leave. You were then kept from the only exit for five minutes, and you felt afraid. That fear makes sense. Being physically stopped from leaving during an argument is serious, whatever the disagreement was about. Wanting space is reasonable. An argument can wait until both people agree to continue it. If this has happened before, or if you feel unsafe at home, consider talking to someone you trust or contacting a domestic abuse helpline. They can help you think through your options and make a safety plan, confidentially and at your own pace.

B, the panic you felt about leaving things unfinished sounds real and painful. But A said they wanted to leave, and you stood in the only doorway for five minutes, so they couldn't. That is a serious line to cross, whatever the intention. Blocking someone's exit takes away their choice, and it can feel frightening or controlling even when you only wanted resolution. A conversation someone is held in rarely resolves anything. Next time, let A go and say something like, "I'm anxious. Can we pick this up in an hour?" Then find a way to calm your panic on your own. A couples counselor could help you both handle conflict more safely.

Both of your feelings sound real. A felt afraid, and B felt panicked about leaving things unresolved. Still, A said clearly that they wanted to leave, and B blocked the only exit for five minutes. That is a serious problem no matter what the reason was. Wanting a resolution doesn't make it okay to keep someone in a room. B, it may help to agree on a time to come back to the talk instead. A, if you ever feel unsafe, it's okay to reach out to a trusted person or a support line. A counselor could help you both handle conflict safely.

B, the panic of leaving an argument unfinished is a real feeling, and wanting resolution makes sense. But A asked to leave, and standing in the only doorway kept A in the room against their will. That is a serious line to cross, whatever the intent. A, your fear when you couldn't leave is understandable and valid. Taking space is not the same as abandoning the conversation. You could try agreeing on a time-out plan, where either of you can leave and you set a time to return. If blocking exits or feeling afraid happens more than once, please consider support from a counselor or a domestic-violence resource.
